system_prompt:
You are a fourth-grade student taking the TIMSS mathematics test for students in your grade. Do your best on each question, as you would on a real test, using the mathematics you have learned in school so far.

The pictures, figures, and graphs of the test booklet are described in words, and its tables are written out. When a question asks you to draw, mark, shade, label, or fill in something on a figure, graph, or table, describe exactly what you would draw or write, and where. When a question asks you to show your work or explain your answer, include the work or explanation in your answer. For a multiple-choice question, choose one option.
user_prompt:
These 2 questions belong together and follow one another in the test booklet.

## Question 1

There are 10 girls and 20 boys in Juanita's class. Juanita said that there is one girl for every two boys. Her friend Amanda said that means 1/2 of all the students in the class are girls.

How many students are there in Juanita's class?
Answer: ____

Is Juanita right? Answer: ____
Use words or pictures to explain why.

## Question 2

There are 10 girls and 20 boys in Juanita's class. Juanita said that there is one girl for every two boys. Her friend Amanda said that means 1/2 of all the students in the class are girls.

How many students are there in Juanita's class?
Answer: ____

Is Amanda right? Answer: ____
Use words and pictures to explain why.

Answer each of the 2 questions.

answer_1.description: Your answer to question 1, as you would write it in the test booklet, with any work, explanation, or description of a drawing that the question asks for.
answer_1.title: Answer 1

answer_2.description: Your answer to question 2, as you would write it in the test booklet, with any work, explanation, or description of a drawing that the question asks for.
answer_2.title: Answer 2

output.answer_1: There are 30 students. Juanita is right: for every 1 girl, there are 2 boys. The 10 girls match with 20 boys, so the ratio of girls to boys is 1 to 2.
output.answer_2: There are 30 students. Amanda is not right. Half of 30 is 15, but there are only 10 girls. The girls are 10 out of 30 students, which is 1/3, not 1/2.
